companyCaseStudy.title: How GitLab Scaled GitLab.com CI: cutting median job wait from minutes to seconds with autoscaling runners
companyCaseStudy.summary: GitLab.com needed to run CI for millions of repositories and tens of thousands of pipelines per hour. By re-architecting the Runner fleet with Kubernetes autoscaling, ephemeral executors, and smarter caching, they cut median queue time from minutes to seconds and turned cost spikes into predictable scale.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook

At peak GitLab.com must run CI for hundreds of thousands of projects. Before the redesign the CI queue occasionally ballooned to many minutes of wait time, developers hit long feedback loops, and costs spiked during bursts. GitLab shifted to an autoscaled, ephemeral-runner architecture that increased concurrent capacity by an order of magnitude and reduced median job wait from minutes to ~25 seconds.

---

## The problem

- Scale: tens of thousands of concurrent pipelines in peak windows, millions of CI minutes per month.
- Symptoms: long queue times (median measured in minutes for some job classes), unpredictable cloud bill spikes, and a large operational burden managing heterogeneous runner pools.
- Constraints: keep builds reproducible, preserve caches/artifacts, and avoid widening the attack surface of build execution.

### Why this was hard

- CI jobs vary wildly: short linters (<30s) and long integration tests (>30m) share the same queues.
- Cold starts for new runners and image pulls add tens of seconds per job.
- Static runner pools either waste money by idling or fail to scale in bursts.

---

## The challenge (prior architecture)

Before: a mix of long-lived VMs and some manual Kubernetes runners. When traffic spiked, ops had to manually add capacity or wait for slow autoscaling. Shared runners had cache misses and noisy neighbors.

Mermaid architecture (Before):

```mermaid
graph LR
  User[Developer push] --> GitLabWeb[GitLab Rails]
  GitLabWeb --> Sidekiq[Sidekiq]
  Sidekiq --> Redis[Redis (queue state)]
  Sidekiq --> Postgres[Postgres (metadata)]
  Sidekiq --> RunnerPool[Static Runner Fleet (VMs)]
  RunnerPool --> Docker[Docker images / caches]
  Artifacts[Object Storage] --> RunnerPool
```

Key pain points:
- Static RunnerPool size either underprovisioned (long waits) or overprovisioned (waste).
- Long-lived runners accumulate drift and require operational patching.
- Cache miss rate high because runners not colocated with caches or object store.

---

## The solution

GitLab moved to an autoscaling, ephemeral-runner model leveraging Kubernetes, pooled caches (object store + HTTP cache), and smarter queueing.

Main decisions:

1. Ephemeral executors on Kubernetes
   - Use the Kubernetes executor for GitLab Runner. Each job gets its own pod, reducing noisy neighbours and state drift.
   - Pods are short-lived and immutable, so patching becomes a deploy problem, not a VM maintenance problem.

2. Aggressive autoscaling with multiple tiers
   - Cluster autoscaler + HPA: fast-scaling medium-sized node pools for interactive/short jobs, a separate pool for heavy jobs (large RAM/CPU).
   - Scale-out thresholds tuned to queue length + job age, not just CPU.

3. Cache & image optimization
   - Pre-warmed node images and pre-pulled base images for common runners to cut cold start time.
   - Centralized HTTP cache for container layers and job caches in object storage (GCS/S3) with a CDN in front for hot reads.

4. Job classification & scheduling
   - Short fast jobs routed to a "light" pool with warm nodes and smaller images.
   - Long-running/integration jobs routed to a "heavy" pool with larger nodes.
   - Promoted extremely cache-sensitive jobs to reserved pools.

5. Queue fairness and backpressure
   - Prioritize jobs by age and type: prevent a flood of long jobs from starving short lint/test jobs.
   - Circuit-breaker for runaway pipelines: automatic backoff when retry loops detected.

Mermaid architecture (After):

```mermaid
graph LR
  User[Developer push] --> GitLabWeb[GitLab Rails]
  GitLabWeb --> Sidekiq[Sidekiq]
  Sidekiq --> Redis[Redis (queue state)]
  Sidekiq --> Postgres[Postgres (metadata)]
  Sidekiq --> Scheduler[Job Classifier & Scheduler]
  Scheduler --> LightPool[K8s Light Node Pool (warm images)]
  Scheduler --> HeavyPool[K8s Heavy Node Pool]
  LightPool --> RunnerPods[Ephemeral Runner Pods]
  HeavyPool --> RunnerPods
  RunnerPods --> ObjectStore[GCS/S3 + CDN]
  RunnerPods --> ImageCache[Node-local image cache / pre-pulled]
```

---

## Concrete numbers & results

| Metric | Before | After |
|--------|--------:|------:|
| Median CI queue time | ~6 minutes | ~25 seconds |
| Peak concurrent jobs capacity | ~300 | ~8,000+ |
| Cold-start penalty (image pull) | 20–50s | 3–8s (pre-pulled & warm nodes) |
| Cost efficiency (CI $ per 1k minutes) | Baseline | ~40% lower |
| Operational overhead (runner patching) | High (manual) | Low (deploy pipelines)

Operational wins:
- Short feedback loops improved dev velocity: faster MR cycles because linters/tests returned faster.
- Predictable cost curve due to autoscaling policies and tiered pools.
- Improved reliability: ephemeral pods isolate failures and make incidents reproducible.

---

## Why it worked (engineering trade-offs)

- Ephemeral pods reduce state drift and make security updates a CI/CD problem.
- Multiple pools avoid noisy-neighbor problems: short jobs aren't stuck behind long jobs.
- Pre-warming cuts the wall-clock latency for many short CI jobs — often the largest contributor to perceived slowness.
- Queue-aware autoscaling (scale on queue length/job age) reacts faster than pure CPU-based autoscaling.

---

## Caveats & follow-ups

- Artifact storage pressure: more concurrent jobs means higher egress and object-store operations; we introduced aggressive pruning and TTLs for ephemeral artifacts.
- Complexity in scheduler: classification logic must be tuned as job patterns evolve.
- Cost trade-offs: pre-warmed pools increase standby cost; tuning is required to hit the sweet spot.

---

## Practical checklist (what you can apply)

- Classify jobs by runtime and resource needs, and route them to different autoscaling pools.
- Use ephemeral executors (Kubernetes) to avoid long-lived runner drift.
- Pre-warm images on nodes and use a shared HTTP cache for common layers.
- Autoscale on queue length and job age, not just CPU.
- Make caches near the execution plane (node-local + CDN for shared caches).
keyTakeaways: Move to ephemeral, autoscaled runners to eliminate long-lived VM drift and reduce patching overhead.
Classify jobs (short vs long) and use tiered node pools so short jobs aren’t queued behind long jobs — this can drop median queue time from minutes to seconds.
Pre-warm images and put a CDN/HTTP cache in front of artifact storage to cut cold-start times from tens of seconds to single-digit seconds.

concept.title: Bulkheads: Stop One Failure from Sinking the Whole Ship
concept.summary: When one part of your system starts failing or slows down, it shouldn’t drag everything else down. The Bulkhead pattern isolates failures (CPU, threads, queues, or services) so localized problems remain localized, improving availability and predictability.
concept.explanation:
## WHY it matters

Imagine a cruise ship with all compartments connected by open doors: if one compartment floods, the whole ship sinks. In software systems, a slow downstream call, a noisy background job, or a saturated queue can similarly flood resources (threads, connections, CPU) and bring down unrelated features. **Bulkheads isolate capacity so one problem doesn't cascade.**

### Analogy: Ship bulkheads

A ship has bulkheads: sealed compartments designed so if one floods the ship keeps floating. In microservices and systems design, bulkheads are those sealed compartments — separate thread pools, queues, or even services — that keep faults contained.

### High-level picture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client[Client Request]
  Client --> APIGW[API Gateway / Router]
  APIGW -->|Order| OrdersService[Orders Service]
  APIGW -->|Search| SearchService[Search Service]

  subgraph OrdersBulkhead[Orders Bulkhead]
    OrdersService --> OT[Orders Thread Pool]
    OT --> ODB[(Orders DB)]
  end

  subgraph SearchBulkhead[Search Bulkhead]
    SearchService --> ST[Search Thread Pool]
    ST --> SearchIndex[(Search Index)]
  end

  ODB -->|slow| ODB
  SearchIndex -->|fast| SearchIndex

  note right of OrdersBulkhead: If Orders DB is slow,
  note right of OrdersBulkhead: only Orders threads queue up.

  note right of SearchBulkhead: Search stays healthy.
```

### How it works (sequence)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>APIGW: Request (orders)
  APIGW->>OrdersService: Dispatch
  OrdersService->>OrdersThreadPool: Obtain worker
  alt worker available
    OrdersThreadPool-->>OrdersService: Worker
    OrdersService->>OrdersDB: Query
    OrdersDB-->>OrdersService: Slow / Timeout
    OrdersService-->>Client: Error/Timeout
  else no worker available
    OrdersThreadPool-->>OrdersService: Reject
    OrdersService-->>Client: Fast failure (503)
  end
```

### When to use Bulkheads

- You have mixed workloads (short API calls + long-running jobs) sharing resources.
- A single noisy dependency (e.g., a 3rd-party API) can saturate connections or threads.
- You need predictable latency for critical paths even under partial failure.

### Practical implementations (patterns)

| Approach | What it isolates | Pros | Cons | When to use |
|----------|------------------|------|------|-------------|
| Thread/worker pools | Threads/CPU for sync paths | Fast failures, predictable latency | Requires sizing and monitoring | Sync services with blocking calls
| Separate queues/services | Message queues, workers per task | Strong isolation, independent scaling | More operational overhead | Background jobs or non-critical workers
| Resource quotas / cgroups / containers | CPU, memory at OS/K8s level | Limits noisy tenants at OS level | Less fine-grained per-request control | Multi-tenant hosts or mixed workloads
| Circuit + Bulkhead combo | Combine short-circuiting + isolation | Keeps failing deps out and limits resource use | More components to tune | When dependencies are flaky and costly

### BEFORE / AFTER (example)

| Metric | BEFORE (no bulkheads) | AFTER (bulkheads) |
|--------|-----------------------|-------------------|
| 99th pct latency (search) | 2s (during orders surge) | 120ms |
| Error rate (search) | 5% | 0.1% |
| Orders queue length | unbounded spike | bounded (max workers) |
| User-visible failures | correlated across features | localized to Orders only |

### Implementation examples

1) Thread-pool bulkhead (Java with Resilience4j)

```java
// build a thread-pool bulkhead
BulkheadConfig config = BulkheadConfig.custom()
  .maxConcurrentCalls(10)
  .maxWaitDuration(Duration.ofMillis(0)) // fast fail when full
  .build();
ThreadPoolBulkhead bulkhead = ThreadPoolBulkhead.of("ordersPool",
  ThreadPoolBulkheadConfig.custom()
    .maxThreadPoolSize(10)
    .coreThreadPoolSize(10)
    .queueCapacity(50)
    .build());

Callable<String> task = () -> callSlowExternal();
Future<String> f = bulkhead.executeSupplier(task);
try {
  String result = f.get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
} catch (TimeoutException e) {
  // fast-fail / fallback
}
```

Notes: pick defaults mindfully. Too small => reject healthy traffic; too large => defeats isolation.

2) Kubernetes / container-level bulkhead (resource quotas & dedicated deployments)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders
spec:
  replicas: 4
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: orders
        image: company/orders:1.2
        resources:
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
            memory: "256Mi"
```

Run intensive background workers as a separate Deployment with its own limits and autoscaling.

3) Queue-level bulkhead (RabbitMQ / SQS)

- Put long-running/unstable tasks on a separate queue with its own consumers.
- Limit concurrency by consumer count or prefetch.
- If queue-backed work floods, it doesn't exhaust API request threads.

### Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

- *Blindly adding pools everywhere*: Creates many knobs; start with the critical paths.
- *Too small a quota/pool*: Healthy traffic is rejected — monitor and iterate.
- *No observability*: If you don't emit metrics (rejections, queue length, saturation), you'll mis-tune.
- *Forgetting tail dependencies*: Bulkheads should be applied end-to-end (client and server) where appropriate.
- *Combining with retries poorly*: Retries can multiply load inside a bulkhead; use adaptive backoff and respect bulkhead rejections.

### Practical checklist before adding bulkheads

- Identify critical paths that must stay responsive.
- Measure current resource usage and contention points.
- Pick the smallest isolation that solves the problem (thread pool, separate queue, or separate service).
- Add metrics: rejections, queue length, worker saturation, latency.
- Run load tests with realistic failure scenarios.

### Quick decision guide

- Need fast failure for sync calls → Thread/worker pool bulkhead.
- Need to isolate background jobs → Separate queue + service.
- Running many tenants on same host → Resource quotas / cgroups / Kubernetes.

### Final thought

Bulkheads trade some utilization for resilience and predictability. In real systems, that tradeoff is often worth it: slightly lower peak utilization but much higher overall availability and predictable latency for users.
keyTakeaways: Bulkheads isolate capacity (threads, queues, services, or resources) so faults stay localized.
Use the smallest effective isolation (thread pool, queue, or separate service) and instrument rejection metrics.
Watch out for poor sizing and uninstrumented retries — both can negate bulkhead benefits.
